rv.q: Dark and dazzling production exposes singer's late career for the haunted circus it was

Into this tuneful cauldron slinks the man himself, black fedora pulled low on forehead, and from the opening seconds of Myles Frost’s astonishing performance we understand that we are in the presence of something rare and special.
Wheeldon doesn’t stint on the big numbers – although he keeps us waiting for a nightmarishly reimagined Thriller in which Jackson is stalked by carnivalesque grotesques and a leering ringmaster.
MJ the Musical is a sterilised swirl through the life of the King of Pop, but in reality, it is no black or white tale.
The evening boils down to a decent Michael Jackson impersonator doing song and dance routines, padded out with an inert storyline, trite dialogue and hagiographic characterisation.
Never mind “Don’t Stop ’Til You Get Enough”: Christopher Wheeldon’s turbo-charged company hardly pause for breath in this epic thriller of a tribute.
This is very much MJ the Musical’s goal

For all that this musical tries to drop ambiguous hints about MJ’s “achievements” never being forgotten, or argues that he is fighting demons no mere mortals can understand and should be indulged and forgiven, MJ The Musical feels at best like special pleading, at worst, as a copout.
This is a jukebox jubilation and, as such, triumphantly succeeds in recreating a glimpse of a unique and towering talent.

cn.t: Dazzling choreography and electric musical numbers can't mask a sanitized, soulless biography that sidesteps Jackson's controversies. Critics praise the spectacle but lament the evasive, surface-level storytelling.
